title: Paginated reports in Power BI support outbound access protection (Preview)
text: Paginated reports can combine data from Power BI semantic models and other data sources with external resources such as maps and images. Workspace admins can control which destinations the Power BI service can reach when it renders these reports. Paginated reports now support workspace outbound access protection (OAP). When a workspace admin enables OAP for a Fabric workspace, outbound connections from paginated reports are blocked by default. The workspace admin can then create OAP exception rules to allow the connection types and destinations that the reports in that workspace are supposed to access. Why control outbound access at the workspace level? OAP helps workspace admins reduce unintended outbound access when the Power BI service renders paginated reports. Report authors define the data and content their reports need, and workspace admins decide which connections to allow. Authors can keep designing print-ready operational, financial, and regulatory reports using approved connections. How OAP applies to paginated report connections A paginated report might query a Fabric lakehouse or an Azure SQL database for transaction data, query a Power BI semantic model for business metrics, and retrieve images from an external host. The Power BI service makes these requests when it renders the report. Depending on the source, the service can use a cloud connector, a configured data gateway, or a Web connection. The service, not the viewer’s browser, retrieves external images. OAP checks these outbound requests against the workspace’s data connection rules. If a required data source isn’t allowed, the report can’t retrieve data from that source. The following screenshot shows the error Power BI displays when OAP blocks a required connection. Figure: Unable to render a paginated report because OAP blocked data source access. If OAP blocks an external image or map, that resource might not display. The rest of the report can still render if its required data sources are available. Configure only the connections your reports need Start by identifying the connections the Power BI service needs to render your paginated reports. Review each report definition and its configured connections for data sources, semantic models, gateways, map services, and external image hosts. Embedded images don’t require an external request, but images referenced by URL do. Next, enable OAP for the workspace and add data connection rules for the required connectors and destinations. For example, use the SQL Server connector for a Fabric SQL analytics endpoint and the Web connector for maps and external images. For a report that queries a Power BI semantic model, use the Analysis Services connector and an XML for Analysis (XMLA) connection string so the report-to-model connection follows the workspace’s OAP rules. If a paginated report queries a semantic model in another workspace, allowing the report-to-model connection doesn't allow the model to connect to its underlying data sources. Those connections are governed separately by the semantic model workspace's outbound access policy, if enabled. In the following screenshot, you can see an example of an OAP policy with multiple exceptions, enabling a paginated report to pull data from Fabric Lakehouse and warehouse sources, query a semantic model, and fetch content from Web destinations. Figure: An OAP policy with multiple exceptions for a sample paginated report. After the policy takes effect, run a representative report in a test workspace. Check data retrieval and any parameters, subscriptions, maps, or external images the report uses. Confirm that destinations without an applicable rule remain blocked. Next steps Learn more about the feature in the Workspace outbound access protection overview . Follow the step-by-step setup in Enable workspace outbound access protection . Share suggestions on the Fabric Ideas site. Ask questions in the Fabric Community .

title: Workspace outbound access protection for Power BI semantic models and interactive reports (Generally Available)
text: Workspace outbound access protection (OAP) is generally available for Power BI semantic models and interactive Power BI reports in Microsoft Fabric workspaces. With OAP, workspace admins can limit which data sources semantic models reach. They can also limit which semantic models in other workspaces interactive reports can query. These rules help reduce unintended outbound access and mitigate data exfiltration risks. Semantic model creators choose their data sources. Report authors choose their semantic models. Workspace admins decide which outbound connections they want to allow in their workspaces. You can have semantic models and reports in the same workspace if you don’t need strict governance controls. You can also place them in separate workspaces if you don’t want to give report authors direct access to the underlying data sources of the semantic models. Which workspace controls each connection An interactive report can always query a semantic model in its own local workspace. For a model in another workspace, however, the report workspace admin must add a Power BI Semantic Model exception to the report workspace’s OAP policy. The exception applies to the report workspace, not to individual reports. When OAP is on in the model workspace, that workspace’s rules control which data sources the semantic model can reach. Examples include an Azure SQL database, a Fabric lakehouse, or a source reached through a data gateway. Allowing the report-to-model connection in the report workspace doesn’t allow the model-to-source connection in the model workspace, or vice versa. Each workspace enforces its own separate OAP policy. There are some special cases to consider: A semantic model might need an OAP exception even for a lakehouse or warehouse in the same workspace because SQL and ADLS Gen2 connections are considered external connections even if the destination is in the same Fabric workspace. Check the model’s data sources and the connection types to determine the required OAP exceptions. For interactive Power BI reports, note that OAP only governs the connection to the semantic model. OAP does not apply to outbound requests originating from features rendered in the user’s browser, such as an ImageURL or a custom visual. To control browser connections, you must rely on firewalls and other the security controls in your local network. Example: Finance reports use a shared semantic model A finance team publishes interactive reports for regional controllers. The reports use a shared semantic model in a separate analytics workspace. Model owners maintain revenue and expense measures there. The semantic model uses DirectLake over OneLake against an approved Fabric warehouse. The reporting workspace admin adds a Power BI Semantic Model exception for the analytics workspace. The analytics workspace admin adds a separate rule for the SQL Fabric warehouse. Looking at the data connections of the semantic model, the analytics workspace admin can see that the model uses an ADSL Gen2 connection to access the Fabric warehouse data. (Side note, for DirectLake over SQL it would be a SQL connection against the warehouses SQL endpoint.) The diagram shows which workspace controls each connection. Figure: The reporting workspace allows access to the shared semantic model. The analytics workspace allows Direct Lake access to Fabric warehouse data in OneLake. A report bound to a semantic model in an unapproved workspace can’t open because the OAP policy in the report workspace would block the connection. If a semantic model in the analytics workspace wanted to use a different data source, the connection would equally be blocked, refreshes would fail in import mode, queries would fail in DirectQuery mode, and framing would fail in DirectLake mode. The analytics workspace admin must review and approve each new destination separately by adding a corresponding OAP exception. Neither team needs to broaden the other workspace’s rules. The governance controls are managed separately for each workspace. Plan your rollout Before you enable OAP in production, coordinate with report owners, semantic model owners, and workspace admins. Involve gateway admins if needed. Group reports and models with similar connection needs. Check that their connection formats are supported and the required rules are available. Start with a few representative reports and semantic models in a test workspace. Identify where each model resides, which sources it uses, and who owns the connections. You can use Copilot to facilitate and accelerate this process. Then set rules in each workspace. In report workspaces, allow only the other workspaces that host the semantic models your reports need. In the semantic model workspaces, allow only the data sources that the models need. Check model connections even when reports and semantic models share the same workspace. Again, you can use Copilot to facilitate the configuration or use the Fabric REST APIs ( Get Outbound Cloud Connection Rules and Set Outbound Cloud Connection Rules ) directly to manage OAP across multiple workspaces efficiently. After the rules take effect, test reports and semantic models separately. Open a report as a viewer would. Depending on the model, run an Import refresh or a DirectQuery query, or check access to the required Direct Lake tables. Confirm that unapproved destinations stay blocked in the test workspaces. Record why each exception exists and who owns it. Review the rules when you rebind a report, move a model, or change a source endpoint. If a cross-workspace report stops opening after you rebind it, check the report workspace’s exception. If the model can’t refresh or query a source, check the model workspace’s rules. Use Copilot and Fabric REST APIs for efficiency. Next steps Learn more in the Workspace outbound access protection overview and the guidance for semantic models and interactive Power BI reports . Follow the step-by-step setup in Enable workspace outbound access protection . Share suggestions on the Fabric Ideas site. Ask questions in the Fabric Community .

title: On-demand billing for Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
text: Only pay for what you consume Many warehouse workloads are highly variable. In some cases, a few peak periods demand significant compute, while the rest of the month usage is much lower. Shared capacity is a great fit for steady, predictable workloads, while workloads with variable or intermittent demand can benefit from a consumption-based model. On-demand billing for Fabric Data Warehouse gives you that flexibility: you can use dedicated compute when your warehouse needs it and pay for the compute you consume. As introduced in the Fabric on-demand billing platform blog post this new billing model applies more broadly across Fabric. In this post, we'll go deeper on what it means specifically for Fabric Data Warehouse, including when to use it, how it works, and how to get started. What's different With on-demand billing in Fabric Data Warehouse: Isolate Data Warehouse compute from other Fabric workloads to avoid noisy neighbor problems Right-size compute independently for each workspace. Pay for the compute your warehouse consumes Get predictable behavior at the workspace ceiling, with queries queued instead of throttled On-demand isn't a rip-and-replace; it's designed for warehouse workloads that benefit from consumption-based compute. You can use on demand for Data Warehouse while continuing to use shared capacity for other Fabric workloads, allowing you to choose the model that best fits each workload. One thing worth stressing: on-demand billing introduces a new billing construct for Data Warehouse. It doesn't change how compute is provisioned, the backend architecture, or how users interact with the warehouse. What changes is how warehouse compute consumption is billed and controlled. Two capacity models, one platform Shared capacity and on demand complement each other. The right model depends on the workload scenario: Shared capacity On-demand billing Best for Steady, predictable workloads Variable, bursty, or intermittent warehouse workloads Example Scenarios Dashboards, pipelines, and warehouse workloads with consistent demand Month-end processing without sizing for peak demand throughout the month, intermittent development/test workloads without sizing for peak, or bursty production warehouse workloads that benefit from isolation You pay for Provisioned capacity Compute consumed by warehouse Isolation All workloads share the same capacity Warehouse compute is isolated from other Fabric workloads Guardrails Capacity SKU size 24-hour compute limit + workspace ceiling For example, you can keep Power BI and pipelines on shared capacity while moving a warehouse with highly variable demand to on-demand billing. This lets you choose the billing model that best fits each workload. What changes when you turn it on When a capacity admin enables on-demand billing for Data Warehouse, every workspace in the capacity with a warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint begins consuming compute separately from the base capacity. Warehouse consumption also shows up as its own line item on your Azure bill, so capacity admins stop asking, "What was that F256 spike?" and start reading a bill that maps to actual work. Control how much compute each workspace can use On-demand billing gives administrators control over the maximum compute available to each workspace through a workspace compute ceiling. This lets you right-size compute for each workspace based on its workload requirements. A useful mental model is to think of it like a road trip: your workspace compute ceiling is how fast you can drive. Set a higher ceiling when a workspace needs more compute for peak demand, or a lower ceiling when its requirements are more predictable. Unlike a car, setting a higher ceiling doesn't mean you pay for it continuously. You pay for the compute you actually consume, not for the ceiling you've configured. This means you can set the ceiling high enough to accommodate peak bursts without paying for that maximum continuously. For additional cost control, administrators can also configure a spend limit that limits overall consumption within a 24-hour period. The following illustration shows how to configure on-demand billing 24-hour compute limit and workspace compute ceilings for Data Warehouse. Figure: Configuring on-demand 24-hour compute limit and workspace compute ceilings for Data Warehouse. Give every team a lane Workspace ceilings turn a single Fabric capacity into a multi-tenant compute environment for the warehouse. For example, your admin can assign the finance team a 256 CU lane for month-end close; the marketing team a 128 CU lane for segmentation; and the data science team a 512 CU burst lane for ad-hoc modeling. They all run on the same on-demand meter, but nobody's month-end close slows down because marketing kicked off a segmentation query. This provides predictable isolation between teams. How it behaves in practice When you use on-demand billing, Fabric automatically manages several aspects of workspace compute and query execution: Sensible defaults out of the box. Each workspace starts with a smart compute ceiling that mirrors the throughput you'd get with bursting on shared capacity. Admins can tune it per workspace later if needed. No throttling at the workspace ceiling. Queries that don't fit shrink-fit first, get queued, and only return an error if a single query needs more than the entire ceiling. GPU query acceleration is supported. Give acceleration-heavy workspaces a higher ceiling so they aren't throttled before they benefit. Custom SQL pools work as-is. The workspace ceiling becomes the pool able compute; the system pool auto-reserves ~⅓ and you allocate the rest. Monitoring what's actually happening On-demand billing consumption shows up in the Fabric Capacity Metrics app on a dedicated tab, alongside every other billing category on the capacity. Because there's no 24-hour smoothing on this tab, the graphs reflect real peaks and scaling activity that is useful for setting the right workspace ceiling and spend limit for the capacity. The following query shows whether a pool is running on shared capacity or on-demand billing, based on `current_workspace_capacity` column in `sql_pool_insights` view. SELECT sql_pool_name, current_workspace_capacity, is_pool_under_pressure, timestamp FROM [your-warehouse-name].[queryinsights].[sql_pool_insights] ORDER BY timestamp DESC; How to estimate your on-demand bill (quick method) Start with your previous month’s Data Warehouse spend on shared capacity and apply the on-demand multiplier: Estimated Data Warehouse on-demand cost ≈ last month Data Warehouse cost (from Azure bill) × 1.3. Estimated total cost ≈ shared-capacity cost for non-Data Warehouse workloads + (1.3 × last month Data Warehouse cost). Getting started If you're a capacity admin on a Fabric capacity with an eligible subscription: Open the Fabric admin portal, go to Capacity settings, and select your capacity. In the On-demand billing section, enable Data Warehouse. Set a 24-hour compute limit that reflects your budget for the category. Set the default compute ceiling for new and migrated workspaces Adjust the ceiling on any existing workspaces based on requirements. Detailed steps, including how to size a workspace ceiling and how to allocate custom SQL pools, are in the Fabric Data Warehouse on-demand billing configuration guide. The one line to remember On-demand billing gives warehouse teams dedicated compute without requiring additional capacity purchases. Start with a single warehouse workload, monitor consumption patterns, and adjust workspace ceilings as needed. We'd love to hear how you're using it. Share your feedback and experiences in the Fabric Community forum. Next steps Ready to get started? Learn more about on-demand billing for Fabric Data Warehouse, then use the on-demand billing configuration guide to configure workspace ceilings and pools. For additional questions and scenarios, see the on-demand billing FAQ .

title: Fabric on-demand billing and Zero-provisioned (F0) Capacity (Preview)
text: Microsoft is introducing a new way to consume Fabric called on-demand billing . This includes a new F0 SKU , enabling customers to get started with zero upfront commitment, as well as a hybrid option that pairs any traditional F SKU with the flexibility of on-demand billing. In addition to the traditional Fabric capacity model, customers can selectively enable on-demand billing for individual Fabric workloads, such as Data Factory or Data Warehouse, which are broken down into what is known as on-demand billing categories. Customers can set usage thresholds per billing category to maintain predictable governance and spend controls. Ultimately, this gives organizations the flexibility to start with less upfront commitment, adapt to less predictable demand, and balance spiky or outsized workload needs alongside more predictable and contained ones – providing more flexibility in how to consume, manage, and scale usage of Fabric. Flexible capacity models Fabric supports multiple capacity options to match different project stages and needs: Start with F0. F0 is a zero-provisioned capacity SKU with no upfront compute-capacity charge. With this approach, Fabric workloads (billing categories) exclusively use on-demand billing - which can help with evaluation, development / early launch stages, or workloads whose capacity needs are not yet predictable. Add on-demand billing to an F2 or higher capacity. Using SKUs customers have today, they can move Fabric workload(s) of their choice outside of the limits of their shared F-SKU capacity and pay for them separately. All other workloads continue using the provisioned F SKU capacity, making this a practical option where some Fabric workload needs are stable while others are bursty or outsized. Traditional F SKU. This is Fabric’s traditional model where customers can select a capacity size ranging from F2 to F8192 based on their needs. This option remains in-tact alongside the two new ways to consume Fabric outlined above. How on-demand billing works On-demand billing is managed for supported Fabric workloads at the billing category level , ensuring consistent behavior across all workspaces within a capacity. Each category is billed based on actual usage, allowing workloads to scale independently depending on demand. Unlike workloads running from a fixed capacity SKU, on-demand usage is unsmoothed. Capacity administrators can enable on-demand billing for a category from the On-demand billing section on the capacity’s Details tab. Feature: Enable On-demand billing for a category. On-demand consumption is measured in CU-hours (without smoothing). Pricing is based on a multiplier of the pay-as-you-go CU price for any given region, and it varies by billing category from 1x to 3X pay-as-you-go. Storage charges remain separate from compute charges. Note : Autoscale billing for Apache Spark, now re-named “On-demand billing for Apache Spark,” remains generally available and functions as before. Pricing remains unchanged. Example usage scenario An organization running Data Warehouse and Data Factory workloads on a Fabric capacity may choose to place the Data Warehouse category on on-demand billing during a seasonal promotion. Compute intensive Warehouse queries could scale independently while steady workloads continue using the provisioned capacity, without the need for capacity expansion. When demand settles, the administrator can return the category to the shared-capacity model, balancing performance needs with cost efficiency. Spend controls and governance To support cost predictability, administrators can configure spend limits using CU-hours over a rolling 24-hour window . When the limit is reached: New operations are temporarily paused In-flight operations continue until completion Billing resumes automatically once the window resets This provides a safety mechanism for preventing unexpected usage spikes while preserving system stability. Feature: Configure the spend limit for an on-demand billing category. Monitoring on-demand consumption On-demand billing consumption can be monitored using the Capacity Metrics App, in the new “On-demand compute” tab, on a per billing category basis. Feature: Inspect on-demand usage in Capacity Metrics App. Why this matters These updates introduce a more flexible approach to capacity management in Fabric: Lower entry barriers without upfront commitment with F0. Improved cost efficiency by paying only for usage in burst-heavy workloads. Better workload isolation between steady and variable compute patterns. Stronger governance controls through category-level billing and spend limits. Together, these capabilities help organizations modernize infrastructure without over-provisioning capacity or sacrificing control. Learn more For additional details, refer to the Microsoft Fabric documentation on on-demand billing and capacity management .

title: Tune the performance of your medallion pipeline in Fabric Data Warehouse
text: Coauthor - Artur Vieira Part 5 of a series on medallion architecture with Fabric Data Warehouse Measure first, then tune the layer that is actually slow The first four posts covered how to choose a pattern, build the Bronze, Silver, and Gold layers, establish operating rules, and secure each layer for its audience. This final post explains how to identify the source of performance issues and keep pipelines responsive as data volumes and usage grow. Fabric Data Warehouse manages caching, statistics, compaction, and V-Order by default, so you do not manage indexes or distributions as you would in a traditional warehouse. Effective tuning therefore starts with accurate measurement and workload patterns that allow the engine to operate efficiently. Use the following layer-by-layer approach to assess performance. Why this matters In a medallion pipeline, a slow dashboard is not necessarily caused by the Gold layer. The cause might be a cold cache immediately after a refresh, oversized string columns in Silver, or thousands of small files created by a Bronze load. Identifying the affected layer first helps you focus tuning work where it will improve the user experience. The layers help here too. Because each one has a single job, each one also has a typical performance lever: ingestion shape in Bronze, data types and statistics in Silver, and table layout and query shape in Gold. Step 1: Measure before you tune Start with query insights. Each warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint provides views in the queryinsights schema with 30 days of history. Use exec_requests_history to review individual queries, long_running_queries and frequently_run_queries to identify recurring patterns, and sql_pool_insights to investigate warehouse resource pressure. Do not judge a query by its first run. The first execution might load data from OneLake into the cache, create statistics, or resume compute resources. Check the data_scanned_remote_storage_mb column: a nonzero value indicates that the query fetched data from OneLake, while zero indicates that the query was served entirely from cache. Implementation sketch: SELECT TOP 20 distributed_statement_id, label, command, data_scanned_remote_storage_mb, data_scanned_memory_mb, data_scanned_disk_mb, allocated_cpu_time_ms FROM queryinsights.exec_requests_history ORDER BY allocated_cpu_time_ms DESC; Do this well: Label pipeline statements by layer, so you can filter query insights for Bronze loads, Silver transforms, and Gold refreshes separately. Compare repeat runs, not first runs, before deciding a query is slow. Check sql_pool_insights when many queries slow down together. Pressure on the pool is a different problem from one badly written query. Rule of thumb: if you haven't looked at query insights, you're guessing. Step 2: Load Bronze in the shape the engine likes Bronze performance depends largely on how data is ingested. When loading from Azure Data Lake Storage, use COPY INTO and group data into files between 100 MB and 1 GB. If you load multiple Bronze tables, run separate COPY INTO statements in parallel to improve throughput. Avoid trickle inserts, updates, and deletes. Each small write produces a new Parquet file, which fragments the table and makes later reads slower. Fabric Data Warehouse compacts small files automatically in the background, but performance can degrade until compaction catches up. Avoid creating unnecessary small files by pre-staging data and loading it in larger operations. V-Order is another consideration for Bronze. It is enabled by default and can improve read performance with a small ingestion overhead. For a write-heavy staging warehouse, you can disable it. A common pattern uses a staging warehouse with V-Order disabled for raw ingestion and a V-Order-enabled warehouse for Silver and Gold. Do this well: Pre-stage data and insert it in one statement rather than many small ones. Keep imported files between 100 MB and 1 GB when possible, and use Parquet instead of CSV for files that will be queried repeatedly. Leave V-Order on unless you have tested a write-heavy workload and accept that you can't turn it back on. Rule of thumb: a Bronze load that creates thousands of tiny files is a Gold performance problem waiting to happen. Step 3: Give Silver precise types and good statistics Silver is where you define the data types used by downstream queries, so it is the most efficient place to choose them carefully. Use the smallest varchar(n) that fits the data instead of varchar(8000) or varchar(max). Use integer types for whole numbers when their range is sufficient; a decimal declared without precision becomes decimal(18,0), which can require more storage than an integer type. Use date and time types for temporal values, and declare columns NOT NULL when the model allows it. Keep data types identical on columns you join or compare. Mismatched types force conversions that cost time on every query. Fabric Data Warehouse creates and maintains statistics automatically at query time, while proactive refresh attempts to update them after data changes. Because automatic creation occurs during query execution, the first query after a large load can incur that cost. If there is a window between the Silver load and the reporting workload, create or update statistics on columns used in joins, filters, and GROUP BY operations so report users do not experience the additional delay. Do this well: Review column types generated by tools or code-first deployments before they reach Silver. Update statistics on key columns after large loads, in the gap before users query. Keep transactions short, always COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and add retry with backoff in pipelines to handle transient conflicts. Rule of thumb: every oversized column in Silver is paid for again in every Gold query. Step 4: Shape Gold for the queries people actually run Gold performance improves when queries scan only the data they need. Pre-aggregate recurring business calculations, return only the columns required by the report, and apply filters as early as possible rather than relying on the client to reduce the result set. For large Gold tables that are repeatedly filtered on the same columns, consider data clustering. You define clustering with CLUSTER BY on up to four columns when you create the table. The engine stores similar rows together, allowing queries to skip files outside the filter range. Data clustering works best on large tables, columns with medium-to-high cardinality, and selective WHERE filters. Equality joins do not benefit, and ingestion requires additional processing because the data is ordered as it lands. Implementation sketch: CREATE TABLE Gold.FactSales WITH (CLUSTER BY (SaleDate, CustomerID)) AS SELECT * FROM Silver.SalesCleaned; Caching does the rest. In-memory and disk caching are always on and fully managed, so frequently used Gold tables are served from cache after the first read. If an executive dashboard must be fast first thing in the morning, run its key queries after the Gold refresh so the cold start happens before users arrive. Do this well: Choose clustering columns from real filter patterns in query insights, not from guesses. Batch Gold refreshes. Clustering works best when DML statements process at least 1 million rows. Use zero-copy table clones for development and test copies of Gold tables. Rule of thumb: Gold should be fast because it's well shaped, not because someone added a hint. Step 5: Keep it fast over time Performance isn't a one-off project. Data grows, new reports appear, and yesterday's well-tuned query becomes today's long-running one. Review long_running_queries and frequently_run_queries regularly, and watch sql_pool_insights for periods of pressure. If you use the hybrid pattern from Part 1, remember that automatic compaction applies to the warehouse, not the Lakehouse. Lakehouse tables accessed through the SQL analytics endpoint still need appropriate maintenance after significant changes. K

title: Scalar User-defined functions (UDFs) in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Generally Available)
text: T-SQL scalar user-defined functions (UDFs) are now generally available in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint. During preview, scalar UDFs gained support for procedural T-SQL and additional query shapes through Expression Block inlining, a technology built to run procedural logic at warehouse scale. A subsequent preview update expanded loop control, large-value data type support, and the query shapes available to scalar UDFs . General availability builds on that foundation with time-dependent functions, AT TIME ZONE, NEWID(), and improved resource estimation for control-flow statements. Data teams can keep time-sensitive and identifier-generation rules in reusable T-SQL rather than duplicating them across application code, orchestration steps, or queries. The authoring model remains unchanged: existing definitions, permissions, catalog metadata, and call syntax continue to apply. What’s new This release adds the following capabilities: Area New capability What it enables Expression Block inlining Time-dependent functions including GETDATE(), GETUTCDATE(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, SYSDATETIME(), SYSUTCDATETIME(), and SYSDATETIMEOFFSET() Time-aware procedural rules across analytical query shapes Expression Block inlining and Scalar UDF inlining AT TIME ZONE Reusable regional and business-time conversion Expression Block inlining NEWID() A new identifier for each evaluated output row Query resource estimation Improved estimation for conditional and iterative work Resource allocation that more closely reflects expected control-flow work You use the same T-SQL syntax for every scalar UDF. Fabric determines the applicable inlining technique from the function definition. Use current time in procedural business rules Many business rules depend on when a query runs. Examples include SLA classification, expiration checks, processing windows, aging bands, and effective-date logic. Expression Block inlining now supports time-dependent functions inside scalar UDF bodies. The following function compares an order's creation time with the current UTC time and returns its SLA state: CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_GetOrderSlaState ( @CreatedUtc DATETIME2(6), @TargetMinutes INT ) RETURNS VARCHAR(20) AS BEGIN DECLARE @CurrentUtc DATETIME2(6) = SYSUTCDATETIME(); DECLARE @TargetUtc DATETIME2(6) = DATEADD(MINUTE, @TargetMinutes, @CreatedUtc); IF @CreatedUtc > @CurrentUtc RETURN 'Not started'; IF @CurrentUtc Use the function to summarize orders by their current SLA state: WITH OrderSlaStates AS ( SELECT OrderId, dbo.fn_GetOrderSlaState(CreatedUtc, TargetMinutes) AS SlaState FROM dbo.OrderProcessing ) SELECT SlaState, COUNT_BIG(*) AS OrderCount FROM OrderSlaStates GROUP BY SlaState ORDER BY SlaState; The time expression is evaluated during query processing. Separate evaluations can observe different clock values, while multiple rows can receive the same value because of clock resolution and execution timing. Use time-dependent functions for time-aware logic, not as a source of unique row identifiers. The same behavior applies when the function is called from supported CTEs, filters, joins, and grouping queries. The rule remains defined once even when different analytical queries consume it. Apply time-zone rules inside scalar UDFs Operational data is frequently stored in UTC but interpreted according to a business or regional time zone. Keeping the conversion in a function avoids duplicating chained AT TIME ZONE expressions across ingestion, reporting, and monitoring queries. Both Expression Block inlining and Scalar UDF inlining now support AT TIME ZONE. The following example showcases the Expression Block path by converting a supplied UTC value to Eastern time: CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_ToEasternTime ( @UtcValue DATETIME2(6) ) RETURNS DATETIMEOFFSET(6) AS BEGIN DECLARE @EasternValue DATETIMEOFFSET(6); SET @EasternValue = @UtcValue AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AT TIME ZONE 'Eastern Standard Time'; RETURN @EasternValue; END; Because Expression Block inlining applies to this definition, the function can be used in the various query shapes supported by that technique. This CTE converts each stored UTC value before the outer query consumes it: WITH LocalOrderTimes AS ( SELECT OrderId, CreatedUtc, dbo.fn_ToEasternTime(CreatedUtc) AS EasternCreatedTime FROM dbo.OrderProcessing ) SELECT OrderId, CreatedUtc, EasternCreatedTime FROM LocalOrderTimes ORDER BY OrderId; The function returns the same DATETIMEOFFSET value as the equivalent direct expression and applies the daylight-saving-time rules associated with the selected Windows time-zone name. Functions using Scalar UDF inlining can use the same clause within that technique's supported function bodies and calling-query shapes. Supporting the clause through both techniques avoids requiring a separate time-zone conversion strategy when a function follows a different inlining path. Generate identifiers for output rows Expression Block inlining now supports NEWID() inside a scalar UDF body. This supports reusable identifier-generation logic that produces a new value for each evaluated output row. CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_NewProcessingId() RETURNS UNIQUEIDENTIFIER AS BEGIN RETURN NEWID(); END; When the function is evaluated over a row set, each row receives a new value: SELECT OrderId, dbo.fn_NewProcessingId() AS ProcessingId FROM dbo.OrderProcessing ORDER BY OrderId; If an executed function path contains multiple NEWID() calls, each evaluated call produces a separate value. Normal variable semantics still apply, assigning NEWID() to a local variable performs one evaluation, while reading that variable again reuses the stored value. NEWID() is evaluated for each output row, including across distributed execution nodes. Match resource estimates to control-flow work Procedural functions can perform different amounts of work depending on their conditional paths and loop iterations. A compact function call does not necessarily represent a small amount of computation. Resource estimation for scalar UDF control flow has improved. The query optimizer can better account for the work represented by conditional paths and loop iterations when determining the resources required by a workload. Existing functions and calling queries receive this improvement without hints or code changes. What's next No hints or syntax changes are required. Existing UDFs gain newly supported capabilities automatically. For current syntax, metadata, and the construct support for each inlining technique, refer to CREATE FUNCTION for Fabric Data Warehouse . For a guided introduction, refer to Create scalar user-defined functions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse . title: On-premises data gateway November 2026 release
text: The November 2026 release of the on-premises data gateway (version 3000.342) continues our commitment to secure, reliable and accessible connectivity between on-premises data sources and Microsoft Fabric services. This release focuses on strengthening gateway security, improving performance and reliability, enhancing diagnostics, and updating underlying dependencies to maintain compatibility with the latest Power Query capabilities. This release gateway brings more reliable data transfers, improvements to Oracle DirectQuery and expanded diagnostics in the gateway setup application to make troubleshooting easier. It also brings compatibility updates for the November 2026 release of Power BI Desktop, so queries run the same way in Power BI Desktop and in cloud refreshes. It also includes improvements to authentication handling, gateway request processing, and resource utilization, helping organizations maintain stable and secure connectivity across enterprise environments. General improvements and fixes The November 2026 gateway release (3000.342) includes several reliability, performance, and operational improvements. Improved authentication reliability: Fixed an issue to ensure service principal token refresh metadata is retained across gateway operations, supporting more consistent authentication behavior. Enhanced gateway message processing: Improved handling of duplicate packet acknowledgments to prevent redundant processing and improve reliability. Optimized memory management: Reduced memory allocation overhead during gateway serialization, helping improve resource efficiency. Improved caching performance: Enhanced caching behavior to minimize redundant operations and improve processing efficiency. Enhanced service stability: Refined request throttling behavior to improve reliability under varying workloads. These updates help deliver a more consistent and reliable gateway experience. Security improvements and updates Security remains a key priority for the on-premises data gateway. The November 2026 release includes dependency updates designed to address identified security vulnerabilities and strengthen the overall security posture of gateway deployments. Key security updates include: Cryptography dependency update: Updated dependencies to address an identified vulnerability associated with System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs. Updated third-party dependencies: Incorporated applicable security and maintenance updates to gateway components. As part of our ongoing commitment to security and reliability, we continuously evaluate and update third-party dependencies. These updates help maintain a secure and stable gateway experience. We encourage customers to upgrade to the latest gateway version to benefit from these security improvements. Feature updates and new capabilities in OPDG: Gateway Dual Relay Dual Relay is a resiliency feature for the On-premises Data Gateway that provides two relay endpoints: a primary relay and a secondary relay in a backup region . If the primary relay becomes unavailable, gateway communication can continue through the secondary relay, provided the gateway can reach it. Following are the benefits of dual relay feature Improves gateway communication reliability and availability. Reduces dependency on a single regional relay. Provides automatic failover capability. Helps minimize service interruptions caused by regional relay failures. Requires no manual activation for eligible gateways. Learn more in the related documentation. Power BI Desktop compatibility This update brings the on-premises data gateway up to date with the November 2026 release of Power BI Desktop. Download on-premises data gateway (standard mode) Download on-premises data gateway (personal mode) With this version of the gateway, reports you publish to the Power BI Service and refresh through the gateway use the same query execution logic and runtime as the November version of Power BI Desktop. Next steps Upgrade to version 3000.342 to get the latest accessibility, configuration reliability and diagnostics improvements. Please share feedback and feature requests through the Power BI Ideas forum to help shape future gateway investments. Thank you!

title: Fabric Data Warehouse at Ignite: Built for AI-era analytics
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Our telemetry shows that agentic analytics has arrived. Agents query, investigate, iterate, test, and drill down without waiting for human input. This machine-paced activity pushes analytical engines built for human-paced workloads to their limits. Fabric Data Warehouse was built from scratch in the 2020s to support this new interaction model, combining highly scalable serverless compute, a resilient lakehouse architecture, and integration across Fabric. At Ignite, we’re building on that foundation for agents and the people who rely on them. The updates focus on performance at agentic scale, better interoperability with AI, and richer capabilities for warehouse development and operations. Scale performance for agentic investigation When queries wait, agentic investigations pause. We’re improving Fabric Data Warehouse performance on three fronts: Fresh OneLake metadata. A faster, more efficient engine. Workload controls that help you balance performance and cost. Keep SQL analytics endpoint metadata fresh The new metadata sync for the SQL analytics endpoint is now generally available. Tables in OneLake are always visible to the SQL analytics endpoint, and queries return fresh data. This release includes: A straightforward upgrade path from existing SQL analytics endpoints. Metadata refreshes within seconds and at query time, so queries always see the latest data. Large object type(LOB) and time travel support. Compatibility with Delta checkpoint V2. Figure: Animated GIF - demonstrating performance of the new SQL analytics endpoint metadata sync. A faster, more efficient engine In recent days we’ve rolled out a rebuilt distributed shuffle to accelerate data movement between query nodes, along with enhanced task scheduling to improve resource use and speed up query tasks. Combined with several earlier innovations, such as distributed bitmap filters and usage-based resource estimation corrections, these changes have improved Fabric Data Warehouse performance by 70% on an industry-standard benchmark[footnoteRef:1] over the past year. Figure: Fabric Data Warehouse performance improvements over time . Controls tailored to your workloads User workloads have varying demands. Some need cached data to stay warm between bursts; others need predictable resource boundaries or acceleration for latency-sensitive analytics. These controls help you make those trade-offs: Cache cooldown (coming in November ) lets you control how long data stays cached at the SQL pool level. Keep data warm between intermittent activity or shorten retention to reduce idle allocation and cost. On-demand billing (Preview) offers consumption-based billing with capacity-level budget controls and workspace-level ceilings. Data Warehouse consumption is separate from other workload categories. When a workspace reaches its ceiling, queries queue and resume as resources become available. Custom SQL pools (Generally Avaiable) , let you set maximum resource shares and separate workloads by application or statement type. Tune SELECT and non-SELECT allocations to match your read/write needs. GPU-based query acceleration ( L imited P review) targets high-concurrency analytical workloads where latency matters, including interactive reporting and AI-driven exploration. Released in August, it delivers roughly twice the performance at one-third lower cost than competing offerings on a 300GB DirectQuery benchmark. Connect Fabric Data Warehouse to the agents you use Develop, query, and operate through AI tools A faster warehouse is even more useful when AI agents can work with it directly. The remote Data Warehouse MCP server gives agents secure high-quality access to your data warehouses . Agent Skills for Microsoft Fabric provide specialized guidance for developing, querying, and operating Fabric items. Together, MCP and Agent Skills bring agent-driven warehouse development, analytics, and operations into the AI tools developers already use. With warehouse-specific capabilities and expertise, agents can carry out end-to-end tasks: explore schemas, write SQL, troubleshoot queries, and manage warehouse workloads. Figure: B ring your own AI tool to Fabric Data Warehouse . Ground answers in shared business context Fabric IQ integration uses ontologies to connect warehouse data with shared business models, concepts, and relationships. This enables Fabric data agents to provide natural-language answers grounded in governed enterprise data. Publish the agents to Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, or custom endpoints to bring insights into the tools where people work and make decisions. Build, operate, and modernize your warehouse with confidence Modern workloads need more than speed and agent access. They also need expressive SQL, clear operational visibility, and dependable tooling for development, governance, and migration. Monitor workloads and troubleshoot queries Workspace monitoring integration, brings warehouses into a shared view and connects workspace-level signals with individual queries. Graphical query plan (coming soon) and Live Query Troubleshooting (Limited Preview) show plans before execution and activity during execution, helping you identify expensive operators and data movement. SQL pool insights enhancements provide near-real-time vNode usage metrics, making compute usage and pool pressure easier to understand. DW monitor enhancements (coming soon) add diagnostic cards that highlight key workload signals and point you to the next troubleshooting step. Operations agent skills help investigate capacity spikes, recommend SQL pools, assess table health, and analyze failures. Write more expressive SQL and simplify development T-SQL enhancements reduce repetition and simplify window-function filtering with FROM-first queries, GROUP BY ALL, and QUALIFY. Regular expressions and analytical aggregates support pattern matching, replacement, and extraction through REGEXP_LIKE, REGEXP_REPLACE, and REGEXP_SUBSTR. For exact and approximate distribution analysis , use MEDIAN, QUANTILE, APPROX_MEDIAN, and APPROX_QUANTILE. User-defined Functions support richer procedural logic with branches, loops, BREAK, and CONTINUE. Eligible functions are inlined, with creation-time checks, actionable errors, control-flow resource estimation, and plan visibility. Fabric User Data Functions integration lets T-SQL call published Python functions to work with APIs, files, configuration, and other Fabric data. Richer data and table support adds VARCHAR(MAX) and VARBINARY(MAX) to the SQL analytics endpoint, supporting text, JSON, logs, and binary content. The SQL web experience introduces table overviews, a no-code table designer, and interactive result visualizations. Redesigned Object Explorer and results grids and improved IntelliSense round out the experience. Figure: Summary of SQL enhancement announcements . Develop, deploy, and govern with greater control Warehouse Clones ( L imited P rivate P review) create point-in-time, read/write environments within or across workspaces and capacities, without an initial full copy. Use them to separate development, testing, reporting, and recovery. Refresh a clone to a newer restore point while retaining its item and endpoint. Sign up to join the Limited Private Preview. Figure: Animated GIF - D emonstrati on of c ross-workspace warehouse cloning in Microsoft Fabric . CI/CD 2.0 with DacFx provides schema-aware deployment and item-definition lifecycle automation for Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint workflows. Use pre- and post-deployment scripts for preparation and validation, and Schema Compare in VS Code to review object differences before deployment. title: Power BI at Ignite: Building on the momentum
text: If you haven't already, read Bogdan Crivat's Microsoft Fabric Ignite blog post for a complete look at our Ignite announcements across Microsoft Fabric. Coming out of FabCon/SQLCon in Barcelona and the Power Platform Community Conference, I'm more excited than ever about what's ahead for Power BI. It's been inspiring to see the community explore new AI-powered experiences and rethink how we interact with data, uncover insights, and make decisions. At FabCon, I shared that Power BI is entering its next chapter. Your ideas, enthusiasm, and feedback since then have helped shape what we're delivering this week. At Ignite, two key parts of that chapter are ready for you to try: Power BI Desktop for Apps and semantic views, both now in public preview. Power BI Desktop for Apps: Build apps where you already build reports In Barcelona, we gave you an early look at a new app-building experience in Power BI Desktop, powered by Fabric apps. This week, it arrives in preview as Power BI Desktop for Apps. It starts where Power BI always has with a semantic model you already trust. Choose a published semantic model, describe the app you want in natural language, and an agent builds it and iterates with you. Refine the result with direct edits and a design pane, preview it locally, and publish it to Microsoft Fabric when it's ready. Because these are apps, they can do more than display data. They can accept inputs, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows. That makes room for everything from a focused portal for a team's reports to a planning app where people enter targets, approve them, and comment in context, all built on the definitions your organization already trusts. Reports aren't going anywhere; they remain the fastest way to explore and share insights. Apps extend what you can build on the same semantic model when people need to act on what they see. This experience isn't limited to Fabric capacity customers. Apps in Power BI are available to Power BI Pro customers in the coming weeks, with support for Premium Per User coming in the months ahead. Fabric apps , the technology underneath, is also now generally available. Figure: Creating an app with the new experience in Power BI Desktop . The apps you build with Power BI Desktop for apps come with a new set of visuals made for Fabric apps. Charts, maps, KPI cards, slicers and data grids share consistent typography, color and spacing, so an app looks cohesive without requiring you to hand-tune every visual. They work in light and dark themes and adapt to your app's own colors. They also behave the way Power BI users expect. With the Fabric visuals packages you get familiar Power BI capabilities like tooltips, cross-filtering and cross-highlighting, so selecting a point in one visual focuses the rest of the page. They support keyboard navigation and screen readers too. To learn more about how we're designing visuals for people and agents alike, refer to the blogpost on Data visualization in the agentic era . Figure: Examples of Fabric visual s capabilities . Semantic views: an open semantic layer, built on Apache Ossie The semantic layer is an organization's most strategic asset. With more than 22 million Power BI semantic models in use every day, Power BI is the world's most widely adopted semantic layer, and the business meaning in those models increasingly grounds agents, apps, and Microsoft Copilot. Today, semantic views enter public preview as the first semantic layer based on Apache Ossie (incubating) open standards, with the unparalleled modeling power of Power BI behind it. You define governed business metrics and semantics directly where your data lives in OneLake, in an open format designed for interoperability. Measures can be written in DAX, so a definition like Total Sales can carry year-over-year and rolling-period logic, not just a simple sum. Define a metric once and reuse it across reports, apps, and AI, within Fabric and, through Apache Ossie, with platforms such as Snowflake and other partners over time. Semantic models remain the heart of Power BI and Fabric IQ. Semantic views complement them by separating business definitions from compute, so the definitions your teams agree on can move across engines and ecosystems without being rebuilt. We'll keep advancing Apache Ossie with Snowflake and the broader community, including establishing DAX as an Ossie-recognized query language. Figure: Defining governed business metrics in a semantic view . What's ahead If you're ready to take the next step and want to learn how to build apps for your teams and organization, we invite you to join Data Days: AI Work​ to learn from practitioners through real projects, working demos, and follow-along sessions. Whether you want to understand the possibilities, find a pattern to try, or share what you build, explore the sessions and find your next step at aka.ms/DataDays . Register for our upcoming Fabric and SQL Community Conferences: Atlanta | Sydney —use code MSCUST to save. Thank you for building with us and for continuing to challenge us to imagine what comes next. I can't wait to see what you create.

title: Run proactive operations with Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. AI is changing how every organization works. For most teams, the hard question isn't whether to use AI. It's how to turn it into real changes in daily operations: fewer surprises, faster responses, and better experiences for customers. Events often arrive faster than any person can respond. In the past, teams were limited by how quickly someone could read an alert and make a call. Now, agents can watch every signal and act in seconds, and each action and its outcome feed back into the system so it improves over time. This isn't only about factory floors or connected devices. Every organization has events it wants to respond to: Catch an issue before it happens, such as a shipment running late or a system nearing capacity. Monitor processes and systems for anomalies, enabling a fix before something breaks. Automate entire workflows instead of handing work between teams. Improve the customer experience while the customer is still engaged. TransGrid Energy uses Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence to turn live data-center telemetry into better operational outcomes. By bringing power, cooling, battery, and equipment data together with real-time alarm rules and its WattSchema ontology, TransGrid can identify potential failures before they happen and optimize cooling or battery use as operating conditions and energy prices change. Data-center operators can improve uptime, efficiency, and cost control without building and maintaining complex data-movement infrastructure. “We want to focus on our business problems, not our data movement problems. Fabric Real-Time Intelligence handles this for us so we can focus on our business” Tony Guidici - CTO / Head of Digital Service, TransGrid Energy, LLC At Ignite, we're announcing new capabilities in Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric that make it simpler to stream, analyze, and act on event data. We're helping our customers move from waiting for something to fail and reacting, to predicting that it might fail and getting ahead of it. Figure: Real-Time Intelligence connects streaming, analysis, and action in a continuous loop. Stream: Connect to real-time data wherever it lives Every organization already has streaming data, from applications, databases, devices, and logs. For years, putting it to work was a project of its own. The data lived across clouds and systems, and every source needed its own pipeline. Ingesting, storing, querying, and alerting each took a separate tool, with its own security model, its own bill, and its own specialists. The cost and complexity stalled many projects before they delivered anything. Real-Time Intelligence changes that. Working with streaming data no longer takes a specialist. With Eventstream , you can connect Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, MQTT, and database change data capture, then filter, transform, and route events without writing code. If it produces events, Fabric can take them. Real-Time hub , built into every Fabric tenant, gives you one place to discover and manage all of it, with nothing to set up. And because it's part of Fabric, streaming data gets the same security, governance, and cost management as the rest of your data. What's new for s treaming Event Hubs shortcuts (Preview) Many teams already run their event pipelines on Azure Event Hubs. We're introducing Event Hubs shortcuts so you can bring an event hub you already run into Fabric as an eventstream, without an extra copy. You keep control in Azure, and you can filter, transform, and route events to Eventhouse, lakehouse, Activator, and more. Native Eventstream routing endpoint in Azure IoT Hub (Generally Available) Many device solutions already send their telemetry through Azure IoT Hub. Eventstream is now a native routing endpoint in IoT Hub, so you can send device data straight into Fabric using the routing rules, filters, and message enrichments you already have. You get from device telemetry to real-time insights, alerts, and automated actions faster, and you can combine telemetry with device-state events for a fuller view of your operations. Figure: Fabric Eventstream is now a native endpoint in Azure IoT Hub for message routing. And you can now attach update policies to accelerated shortcuts, so transformations run continuously as new data lands in the lake, with no separate pipeline. text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Together, these innovations simplify the journey from idea to production and bring greater intelligence to database operations. Move from prompt to production with Fabric apps Fabric apps (Generally Available) , give developers and coding agents a simpler path to building and deploying complete business applications. Developers and coding agents can build Fabric apps with Rayfin, the open-source SDK and CLI that provides backend capabilities including databases, authentication, functions, storage, and observability. Build on trusted enterprise data Fabric apps connect to existing semantic models, warehouses, and lakehouses, allowing developers to build on trusted business data without recreating data models or access controls. Serverless PostgreSQL in Fabric, built for intelligent applications Developers have always built applications on databases, but agents are now building them at an entirely different speed. Agents spin up databases for prototypes, experiments, and short-lived tasks, then drop them when the work is done. Most of these workloads start small, run in bursts, and sit idle between uses, which makes their compute needs hard to predict and inefficient to run continually. Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB is serverless and built for exactly these scenarios, with: Rapid provisioning: Databases provision in seconds so developers and agents can start building immediately. Automatic pause: Compute pauses after five minutes of inactivity to avoid keeping resources running between tasks. On-demand resume: Compute resumes when the next query arrives without manual intervention. Fabric HorizonDB is also available as a PostgreSQL database for Fabric apps. Analytical queries can run an order of magnitude faster or more than they would natively in PostgreSQL. Full and partial pushdown are both supported, so a single query can join PostgreSQL tables with data in OneLake. Mirroring: Fabric HorizonDB tables are replicated into OneLake by default and are automatically converted to Delta format, so data is ready for translytical application workloads and large-scale analytics across Fabric without building data integration pipelines. Synced Tables: Enriched data from Fabric Data Warehouse flows back into HorizonDB (reverse ETL) for low-latency, high-concurrency serving to applications and agents. Snapshot sync handles periodic refreshes such as daily scores or aggregates, while the continuous sync option keeps tables current as source data changes. text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. AI has made it much faster to create an initial version of an app. Ask a coding agent to turn the spreadsheet your team uses to track supplier issues into an app, and it can be running in hours rather than days. Putting that app in front of the business is another matter. It needs a database, sign-in, and access to company data that respects the permissions already in place, and IT needs to know the app exists. Left to wire this up alone, an agent takes the shortest path, which often means copying data where it shouldn’t go or sharing it with people who shouldn’t see it. Multiply that by every team with an agent and you get shadow IT at agent speed. Rayfin and Microsoft Fabric apps address these deployment and governance challenges, and today at Microsoft Ignite, both are generally available. Developers and their agents build with Rayfin, our open-source SDK and CLI. When deployed, the app runs as a Fabric app, next to your data, behind Microsoft Entra sign-in, and under the governance you already have. We want every team to build like a startup and deploy like an enterprise. Since preview, more than 100,000 apps have been created. The whole app, defined in code With Rayfin, the backend lives in the same project as the user interface. You describe your data and who can access it in TypeScript, and Rayfin generates the database and API with those rules enforced. One command, Rayfin up, deploys the whole app to Fabric. We built it this way on purpose. It gives coding agents a consistent development model instead of requiring them to coordinate multiple cloud services independently. And because every app declares its data, permissions, and connections in one place, it’s easier to review and govern. Figure: Rayfin defines app data, APIs, authentication, policies, functions, and hosting for local or Fabric deployment. Every Fabric app can use: Databases: SQL database in Fabric, or the new Fabric HorizonDB (Preview), serverless PostgreSQL for teams and agents that default to Postgres. Authentication and permissions : Microsoft Entra sign-in and per-record access rules. Functions : server-side TypeScript for business logic, integrations, and calls to Microsoft Foundry models. Connectors : direct access to the semantic models, warehouses, lakehouses, and SQL databases you already have in Fabric. Storage : files, images, and documents, stored in OneLake. Observability: metrics, logs, and traces in Application Insights. Because the app is defined in code, developers can use the same project across local and cloud environments. Rayfin Local runs the app and its back end on your laptop, even before you have a Fabric workspace. The Rayfin up command then publishes the same code to Fabric unchanged. The model is similar to developing in Power BI Desktop and publishing to the Power BI service: creators work locally and deploy to a managed service when they are ready to share. That shared development model is already helping organizations reduce the handoffs between data experts and engineers. The Craneware Group , which helps healthcare providers optimize their financial performance, previously lost days or weeks as ideas moved between customers, data experts, engineering, and production. With Fabric apps, its data experts can build alongside engineers on a shared, governed foundation, helping ideas move from review to deployment without the wait. “Fabric apps are changing the way we think about application development. Fabric apps build on that work instead of starting over with another copy. With the new Fabric IQ connector, people can also ask about that data in plain language. And decisions made in the app can be written back to governed tables in OneLake, ready for reporting and AI. That foundation is already changing how teams put trusted data into action. At Thomson Reuters , the Monthly Business Review now runs as a Fabric app, built on the same certified Power BI semantic models that ground the company’s DeepVista AI framework and its agents in Microsoft Teams. By bringing trusted metrics, natural-language analysis, and review workflows into a single experience, the team spends less time reconciling numbers and more time deciding what to do next. “This is a breakthrough in how Finance works. Certified semantic models give us numbers we can trust. Thomson Reuters DeepVista’s AI agents let analysts and leaders ask questions in natural language and get insights they can act on. The monthly business hub solution automates the business review, so we spend our time on what to do next.” —Michael Goddard, Head of Corporate Finance, Thomson Reuters Watch the interview with Thomson Reuters to see how they are innovating with Fabric. Governed by default As more people build with AI, apps will multiply faster than any IT team can review them one at a time. The controls have to live in the platform, not in a review queue. Every Fabric app is a Fabric item, so it shows up in lineage, follows your workspace permissions and sharing rules, and runs on your capacity. Content Security Policy (CSP): control over which external resources an app can load in the browser. Secure Embed: the option to require that apps run only inside an embedded frame. Item identity: apps reach data under their own identity, not the permissions of the person who deployed them. Figure: Manage and govern Fabric apps across your organization with the Apps view in the OneLake Governance hub. Build wherever you work Professional developers will build in code with the agent they prefer. But many of the most useful apps will come from the people closest to the work, like the analyst who owns the forecast. They should be able to start in familiar Microsoft experiences and build on the same governed foundation. Microsoft Copilot: Turn a simple prompt into a working application, with the option to use Fabric as a managed backend for databases, storage, and data APIs through Copilot Managed Runtime. title: OneLake: The unified foundation for data, context, governance, and AI
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Most organizations' data is scattered across dozens of applications, clouds and services. Now that agents need to work across the entire business, organizations need to bring that data together in one place: one copy, open to every engine and team, without moving or duplicating it. Unified data gives agents reach, but to act with confidence they also need context: what the data means, how it connects to the business, who should see it and whether it can be trusted. OneLake is the single place for customers to unify their data estate. Shortcuts , mirroring , catalog federation and IQ Share bring multi-cloud, on-premises sources and databases and data platforms together into a single view of the data estate. The OneLake catalog provides a trusted place for organizations to easily explore, govern and secure data in OneLake. It's integrated with every Fabric workload and one of the only lakes that governs data in both Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg open formats, making it truly open. Users can bring popular analytics and AI products and open-source projects to open data in OneLake. Figure: OneLake provides an open, governed foundation for Fabric workloads. In addition, more than 240,000 organizations use the OneLake catalog to govern more than 350 million data items. The catalog is embedded in more than 100 apps people use every day, including Foundry, Power BI, Teams, and Excel. At Microsoft Ignite, we're taking the next step and making OneLake catalog the center of Microsoft's data governance strategy , delivering new capabilities that bring data, context, and governance together for AI, and expanding the partner ecosystem that extends OneLake across the wider data estate. Here's what that means to you. The OneLake Catalog: Governance where your data lives Customers have told us consistently that running a standalone catalog alongside their data platform creates friction, and that they want governance to live where data is analyzed and put to work. The market has moved the same way, with leading data platforms building governance directly into the analytics experience. Fabric has always had a lake-first data foundation with OneLake, and OneLake catalog already has market leading governance and administration. Figure : OneLake catalog brings data discovery, governance and security together on OneLake, with Copilot built in. This is where Microsoft has strong momentum. We’re making a definitive announcement: OneLake catalog is now Microsoft’s data governance product . This isn't something new either. The OneLake catalog has been the trusted catalog for Fabric data for years, and we're now deepening our investment in it. From a single place, teams can deliver on three main tasks: Explore : Easily discover and understand data across the estate, with lineage, permissions and business context on every item. Govern : See governance insights and recommended actions , and manage domains, tags, endorsements and policies centrally. Secure : Manage OneLake security roles and fine-grained permissions in one central hub . As part of this data governance evolution, Microsoft Purview Data Governance will be retired , and new data governance innovation will land in the OneLake catalog. We want to be clear about what this means. The OneLake catalog takes a different approach: rather than cataloging metadata wherever it lives, it governs the data that lives in or is connected to OneLake through native items, federated catalogs, IQ Shares, Shortcuts and Mirrored databases. That makes it a new model, not a feature-for-feature replacement for Purview Data Governance. Purview Data Security and Compliance, including Information Protection, Data Loss Prevention, Insider Risk Management and Data Security Posture Management, are not affected and continue to protect your data in Fabric. OneLake catalog brings discovery, governance, and security together where data is managed and used. Generally available capabilities help teams find and understand trusted data, monitor governance health, and enforce consistent protections. Govern Skills help identify gaps and prioritize action. We have enhanced further with richer discovery across granular data objects, improved search and lineage, and new Curation and Protection Skills. These skills extend AI-assisted governance beyond health assessments, helping organizations improve metadata quality, identify protection gaps, and take action with AI assistance. Together, these capabilities make it easier to find trusted data, understand how it's being used, and manage governance and security at scale. With Data governance being a core priority for us and our customers – we will continue expanding these capabilities with Data Quality, enhanced curation with glossaries, enhanced granular lineage, additional policies for guardrails, and more. All with the goal to allow governing your data at scale and ensuring your data is ready for AI. Strategic partnership with Atlan to extend data governance Today we are announcing a strategic partnership with Atlan aligned with our lake-first data governance approach. OneLake and Fabric customers can use Atlan, Microsoft’s preferred data governance partner, to extend governance beyond OneLake. The OneLake catalog provides native governance across Fabric and connected data, while Atlan complements it across the broader data estate. Atlan also provides granular, cross-estate lineage and richer governance constructs such as usage and popularity stats across heterogeneous, non-Microsoft data sources, and supports customers transitioning from Purview Data Governance to Fabric with tooling to carry their existing metadata forward. Figure: OneLake and Atlan provide complementary governance across the broader data estate. Governance gives organizations confidence in their data. title: Bringing trusted Fabric IQ context to wherever people and agents work
text: If you haven’t already, read Arun Ulag’s Ignite blog post to learn how Microsoft is bringing together databases, analytics, and intelligent applications across Azure and Microsoft Fabric. Over the past year, AI has moved from answering questions to doing the work. As the 2026 Microsoft Work Trend Index shows, people are now handing entire tasks to agents and directing several at once. Those agents plan, decide, and act across systems, with less human review at every step. Fabric IQ helps turn your organization's business knowledge into an advantage for people and agents. As agents take on more responsibility, that knowledge matters more than which model they run on. Every organization can use the same frontier models. What sets yours apart is its context layer: the definitions, metrics, relationships, and rules that describe how your business actually works. When you connect that context with knowledge from across the organization, people and agents can uncover insights and take informed action that reflects how the business operates. The organizations seeing results treat business context as shared infrastructure, built once and reused by every agent. Today at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we're extending the reach of Fabric IQ, the part of Microsoft IQ that captures how your business operates, to more of the places where that work happens, including Microsoft Copilot, Excel, ChatGPT and Codex by OpenAI, Claude by Anthropic, Fabric apps, and GitHub Copilot. We're also strengthening every foundation beneath it, from Microsoft OneLake and semantic models to ontologies and Fabric agents, so the context your teams define can power every agent that follows. Fabric IQ and Microsoft IQ A common challenge in getting agents into production is that the context, data, models, and runtime they depend on sit in silos, so teams end up rebuilding them for every project. Microsoft IQ , which we're introducing today, is the enterprise context management platform that helps organizations build their own IQ by capturing, governing, and reusing the business knowledge their apps and agents depend on. It connects context from Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ, so every agent starts from what your organization already knows.
